focus: Section 2.1 Batch gradient descent and the role of the learning rate. Explain the update theta <- theta - eta * grad J(theta) on a simple one-dimensional quadratic loss J(theta) = a/2 * (theta - theta_star)^2. Let the learner change the learning rate eta, the curvature a and the starting point, and show the sequence of iterates and losses for a few steps. Guide them through a learning rate that is too small and one that is too large (divergence). Check that with eta*a = 1 the method reaches the minimum in one step and that it diverges when eta*a > 2.
excerpt: 2 Gradient descent variants (paraphrased). Gradient descent minimizes an objective function J(theta) parameterized by a model's parameters theta by updating the parameters in the opposite direction of the gradient of the objective with respect to the parameters, grad_theta J(theta). The learning rate eta determines the size of the steps taken to reach a (local) minimum: we follow the direction of the slope of the surface created by the objective downhill until we reach a valley. 2.1 Batch gradient descent computes the gradient of the cost function with respect to the parameters for the entire training dataset: theta = theta - eta * grad_theta J(theta). Batch gradient descent is guaranteed to converge to the global minimum for convex error surfaces and to a local minimum for non-convex surfaces. 3 Challenges: choosing a proper learning rate can be difficult. A learning rate that is too small leads to painfully slow convergence, while a learning rate that is too large can hinder convergence and cause the loss function to fluctuate around the minimum or even to diverge.
